title: Aerodynamics
tagline: Aerodynamic forces, potential flow, airfoil theory and panel methods, finite wings, viscous drag, shocks and expansions, and transonic and supersonic flow
summary: Aerodynamics explains how wings produce lift and what it costs in drag. The course builds from aerodynamic forces and potential flow to thin-airfoil theory, panel methods, finite wings and induced drag, and viscous effects and stall, and then turns to compressible aerodynamics: oblique shocks and expansion waves, subsonic and transonic airfoils, supersonic flow and the main features of hypersonic flight.
overview: Aerodynamics is the study of the forces that air exerts on bodies moving through it, and of the flows that produce them. It decides how large a wing must be to carry an aircraft, how much fuel the aircraft burns, how fast it can fly before shock waves form, and how hot a re-entering capsule becomes; the same methods are used for wind-turbine and propeller blades, racing cars, bridges and tall buildings. For a wing the central questions are always the same: how much lift, at what cost in drag, and with what pitching moment.

The course is organised by flight regime. The first half treats low-speed flow. It sets up the force and moment coefficients and the similarity parameters $\mathrm{Re}$ and $M$, then builds inviscid theory step by step: potential flow and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem; thin-airfoil theory, which gives the lift slope $2\pi$ and the zero-lift angle and moment of any thin section; panel methods for arbitrary shapes; and Prandtl's lifting-line theory for wings of finite span and their induced drag. A chapter on boundary layers then supplies what inviscid theory cannot: skin friction, profile drag, stall and high-lift devices. The second half treats compressible flow: oblique shocks and Prandtl–Meyer expansions, compressibility corrections and the transonic drag rise with the supercritical airfoil and sweep that delay it, and finally linearised supersonic theory and the main features of hypersonic flow.

What makes the subject hard is that each theory is exact only within its assumptions — thin bodies, small angles, attached flow, a given range of Mach number — and real design work consists largely of knowing which theory to trust and where it fails. Every chapter therefore derives its results, works numerical examples with real units, compares the simple theories with more exact ones or with test data, and points out the limits. Work the examples by hand, use the interactive figures to see how the answers change with the parameters, and check every result against a limiting case.
outcomes: Calculate lift, drag, and pitching moment coefficients and explain their dependence on angle of attack, Reynolds number, and Mach number
Apply potential flow theory, thin-airfoil theory, and panel methods to predict the pressure distribution and forces on airfoils
Explain the origin of induced drag and calculate the lift distribution and induced drag of finite wings using lifting-line theory
Describe boundary layer development on airfoils, predict skin friction drag, and explain the mechanism of stall
Apply oblique shock and Prandtl-Meyer expansion relations to supersonic flow over wedges and airfoils
Calculate the critical Mach number and drag divergence Mach number, and explain how supercritical airfoils and sweep delay the drag rise
Apply linearised supersonic theory (Ackeret theory) to calculate lift and wave drag of thin supersonic airfoils
Describe the main features of hypersonic flow including thin shock layers, high stagnation temperatures, and real gas effects

chapters.title: Aerodynamic forces and coefficients
chapters.summary: Lift, drag and pitching moment and their coefficients, the centre of pressure and the aerodynamic centre, and the similarity parameters of aerodynamics.

chapters.title: Incompressible potential flow
chapters.summary: Stream function and velocity potential, elementary flows and their superposition, flow over a cylinder and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem.

chapters.title: Airfoils and thin-airfoil theory
chapters.summary: Airfoil geometry and nomenclature, the Kutta condition, vortex sheets, and thin-airfoil theory for lift and pitching moment.

chapters.title: Panel methods
chapters.summary: Source and vortex panel methods for airfoils of arbitrary shape.

chapters.title: Finite wings
chapters.summary: Wing-tip vortices and downwash, Prandtl's lifting-line theory, induced drag, and the effects of aspect ratio and sweep.

chapters.title: Viscous effects, drag and stall
chapters.summary: Boundary layers on airfoils, skin-friction and form drag, transition, stall and high-lift devices.

chapters.title: Oblique shocks and expansion waves
chapters.summary: Oblique shock relations, the θ–β–M relation, Prandtl–Meyer expansions and shock-expansion theory.

chapters.title: Subsonic and transonic airfoils
chapters.summary: Compressibility corrections, the critical Mach number, drag divergence and supercritical airfoils.

chapters.title: Supersonic and hypersonic flow

history.title: Circulation and lift
history.detail: Nikolai Joukowski publishes the theorem that the lift per unit span of a body in a stream is the density times the speed times the circulation; Wilhelm Kutta had computed the lift of circular-arc surfaces with a smooth flow off the trailing edge in his 1902 Habilitation work, and Frederick Lanchester had argued for the role of circulation in lift.

history.title: Lifting-line theory
history.detail: Ludwig Prandtl and his Göttingen colleagues publish the lifting-line theory of the finite wing (1918–1919), explaining induced drag and the effect of aspect ratio and showing that elliptic span loading gives the least induced drag.

history.title: Thin-airfoil theory and the Variable Density Tunnel
history.detail: Max Munk's NACA Report 142, General Theory of Thin Wing Sections, gives the zero-lift angle and pitching moment of any thin section as integrals over its camber line; the same year the NACA's Variable Density Tunnel at Langley, which Munk had advocated, first runs, allowing model tests at flight Reynolds numbers.

history.title: Linearised supersonic airfoil theory
history.detail: Jakob Ackeret publishes the linear theory of thin airfoils in supersonic flow, with its lift coefficient 4α/√(M²−1) and the wave drag due to lift and thickness.

history.title: The swept wing
history.detail: At the Volta Conference in Rome, Adolf Busemann proposes sweeping the wings of supersonic aircraft so that the flow normal to the leading edge is slower; the subsonic benefit of sweep was later identified independently by Robert T. Jones of the NACA (1945).

history.title: Faster than sound
history.detail: On 14 October 1947 Charles Yeager flies the rocket-powered Bell X-1 research aircraft beyond Mach 1 over Muroc Army Air Field (now Edwards Air Force Base), showing that controlled flight through the transonic regime is possible.

history.title: The blunt-body principle
history.detail: H. Julian Allen and Alfred Eggers of NACA Ames show that blunt shapes greatly reduce the heating of bodies entering the atmosphere at very high speed, because most of the energy is dissipated in the gas behind a strong detached bow shock; every crewed re-entry capsule follows the principle.

history.title: Panel methods
history.detail: John Hess and A. M. O. Smith at the Douglas Aircraft Company describe the surface-source method for the potential flow about arbitrary three-dimensional bodies, the start of panel methods; their survey of the approach, including lifting flows, appears in 1967.

history.title: The supercritical wing in flight
history.detail: An F-8 research aircraft fitted with a supercritical wing designed by Richard Whitcomb of NASA Langley first flies on 9 March 1971, confirming that a flat-topped, aft-cambered section delays the transonic drag rise; supercritical sections are now standard on transport aircraft.

references.title: Fundamentals of Aerodynamics (6th edition)
references.note: The standard undergraduate text: forces and coefficients, potential flow, thin-airfoil and lifting-line theory, panel methods, and compressible flow up to hypersonic, with many worked examples.

references.authors: I. H. Abbott and A. E. von Doenhoff
references.title: Theory of Wing Sections
references.note: The classic reference for NACA airfoil geometry, thin-airfoil theory and measured section data (lift, moment and drag at several Reynolds numbers).

references.title: Low-Speed Aerodynamics (2nd edition)
references.note: A rigorous treatment of potential flow, singularity distributions, lumped-vortex, vortex-lattice and panel methods.

references.title: Flight Vehicle Aerodynamics
references.note: A modern, compact account of aerodynamic theory as it is used in design, including viscous–inviscid interaction and the boundary-layer methods behind XFOIL.

references.title: Boundary-Layer Theory (9th edition)
references.note: The comprehensive reference on laminar and turbulent boundary layers, transition and integral methods.

references.authors: H. W. Liepmann and A. Roshko
references.title: Elements of Gasdynamics
references.note: A concise and clear treatment of shocks, expansions, linearised compressible flow and the physics of high-speed gases.

references.title: Modern Compressible Flow: With Historical Perspective (3rd edition)
references.note: Oblique shocks, Prandtl–Meyer flow, linearised subsonic and supersonic theory and an introduction to hypersonic flow.

references.title: Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach (6th edition)
references.note: How aerodynamic theory and empirical data (drag build-up, high-lift increments, form factors) are used in conceptual aircraft design.
